steps.title: Four subunits, two dimers
steps.text: Hemoglobin is an α2β2 tetramer: two identical αβ dimers. Each of the four subunits carries a heme, and each heme can bind one O₂.

steps.title: A heme in every subunit
steps.text: The heme iron is held by a histidine — His F8, α87 — on the proximal side. Oxygen binds the iron on the distal side, where a second histidine (E7) helps stabilize it.

steps.title: Oxygen binds the iron
steps.text: In the T state the heme pocket is strained: iron sits slightly out of the porphyrin plane, and oxygen affinity is low. Binding the first O₂ is the hard step.

steps.title: T state: the dimers are locked
steps.text: Salt bridges and hydrogen bonds across the α1β2 interface hold the tetramer in the tense state. The constraints make the first oxygen binding expensive.

steps.title: The α1β1 dimer rotates 15°
steps.text: Oxygen binding at one site breaks the T-state contacts. The α1β1 dimer rotates about 15° relative to α2β2 and slides slightly — the quaternary T→R transition.

steps.title: R state: the other sites bind faster
steps.text: The relaxed state binds O₂ 10–100× more tightly, so the remaining hemes fill quickly. That positive cooperativity is what turns hemoglobin's oxygen curve sigmoid instead of hyperbolic.
